The '''self''' is thus the bit-by-bit product of experience and education: we are what we become - or, in {{w|William Wordsworth|Wordworth's}} later phrase, the child is the father of the man. Particular parents, surroundings and stimuli produce individuated selves. Identity is thus unique because contingent, the cumulative product of ceaseless occurrences. # The [[subject]] of one's own [[experience]] of [[phenomenon|phenomena]]: perception, emotions, thoughts. #* {{RQ:Shakespeare Merchant of Venice|II|ix|text={{smallcaps|Portia}}:
To these injunctions every one doth swear
That comes to hazard for my worthless '''self'''.}} #* {{RQ:Belloc Lowndes Lodger|I|0056 |passage=Thanks to that penny he had just spent so recklessly [on a newspaper] he would pass a happy hour, taken, for once, out of his anxious, despondent, miserable '''self'''. It irritated him shrewdly to know that these moments of respite from carking care would not be shared with his poor wife, with careworn, troubled Ellen.}} # An individual [[person]] as the object of the person's own [[reflective]] [[consciousness]] (plural [[selves]]). #* {{RQ:Hamilton Metaphysics and Logic|chapter=Lecture IX|text=The '''self''', the I, is recognized in every act of intelligence as the subject to which that act belongs. It is I that perceive, I that imagine, I that remember, I that attend, I that compare, I that feel, I that will, I that am conscious.}} #* {{RQ:Maxwell Mirror and the Lamp|chapter=16|passage=The preposterous altruism too!{{...}}Resist not evil. [[away|Away]] from the surface of the [[Earth]] or other [[planet]]; in [[opposite]] direction to the downward pull of [[gravity]]. ##: {{ux|en|I looked '''up''' and saw the airplane overhead.}} ##: {{ux|en|Shoots grow '''up''' and roots grow down.}} ## To or at a physically higher or more elevated position. ##: {{ux|en|All day we climbed '''up''' and '''up'''.}} ##: {{ux|en|Lift the carpet '''up''' and look underneath.}} ##: {{ux|en|He lives '''up''' in the hills.}} ## To an upright or erect position. ##: {{ux|en|sit '''up'''; stand '''up'''; get '''up''' out of bed}} ## {{lb|en|figuratively}} To a higher level of some quantity or notional quantity, such as [[price]], [[volume]], [[pitch]], [[happiness]], etc. ##: {{ux|en|Gold has gone '''up''' with the uncertainty in the world markets.}} ##: {{ux|en|Turn it '''up''', I can barely hear it.}} ##: {{ux|en|Listen to your voice go '''up''' at the end of a question.}} ##: {{ux|en|Cheer '''up''', the weekend's almost here.}} # {{n-g|Indicating movement in any other direction visualised as "up".}} ## To or towards what is considered the top of something, irrespective of whether this is presently physically higher. ##: {{ux|en|Go back '''up''' to the top of the page.}} ##: {{ux|en|As I lay on my back, a pain shot '''up''' from my toes to my chest.}} ##: {{ux|en|Let’s move '''up''' to the front of the bus.}} ## To the [[north]] (as north is at the top of typical maps). ##: {{ux|en|I live in Florida, but I'm going '''up''' to New York to visit my family this weekend.}} ## Towards or at a central place, or any place that is visualised as ‘up’ by virtue of local features or local convention, or arbitrarily, irrespective of direction or elevation change. ##: {{ux|en|We travelled from Yorkshire '''up''' to London.}} ##: {{ux|en|I'm going '''up''' to the other end of town.}} ##: {{ux|en|He lives '''up''' by the railway station.}} ## {{lb|en|rail transport}} Towards the principal [[terminus]], towards [[milepost]] zero. ## {{lb|en|UK|academia|dated}} To university, especially to [[Cambridge]] or [[Oxford]]. ##: {{ux|en|She's going '''up''' to read Classics this September.}} ##* {{quote-book|en|year=1867|author=John Timbs|title=Lives of wits and humourists|page=125 |passage=The son of the Dean of Lichfield was only three years older than Steele, who was a lad of only twelve, when at the age of fifteen, Addison went '''up''' to Oxford.}} ##* {{quote-book|en|year=1998|author=Rita McWilliams Tullberg|title=Women at Cambridge|page=112 |passage=Others insinuated that women 'crowded '''up''' to Cambridge', not for the benefits of a higher education, but because of the proximity of 2,000 young men.}} ##* {{quote-book|en|year=2002|author=Peter Harman|title=Cambridge Scientific Minds|page=79 |passage=A precocious mathematician, Babbage was already well versed in the Continental mathematical notations when he went '''up''' to Cambridge.}} ##
